title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: a night at the arts centre

questions.prompt: The grammar of this lesson names one pattern of its own: noun + past participle, as in science-inspired. Tick EVERY phrase below whose compound adjective is built on that pattern — and only that one.
questions.explanation: Take each compound apart. Glass and hand are nouns, fronted and painted are past participles, so a glass-fronted gallery and a hand-painted poster both follow noun + past participle: the gallery is fronted with glass, the poster painted by hand. The three others each imitate one half of the pattern and miss the other. Badly is an adverb, not a noun, although lit really is a past participle. Winning is an -ing form, so the writer wins prizes instead of receiving the action. And three is a number followed by a plain noun, storey, with no participle anywhere — the same shape as a ten-minute talk.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the two underlined groups with compound adjectives: "They walked down an avenue THAT WAS LINED WITH TREES and stopped by a fountain THAT WAS CARVED FROM STONE."

options.text: a trees-lined avenue and a stone-carved fountain
a tree-lining avenue and a stone-carving fountain
a lined-tree avenue and a carved-stone fountain
a tree-lined avenue and a stone-carved fountain

questions.explanation: Both groups follow the same recipe: the noun goes first, the past participle second, a hyphen joins them and the whole thing moves in front of the noun it describes — a tree-lined avenue, a stone-carved fountain. The noun inside stays singular even when there are hundreds of trees, so "trees-lined" is out. Turning the pair round changes what is described, since "carved-stone" describes stone, not a fountain. And the -ing forms reverse the action altogether: an avenue does not line trees, and a fountain carves nothing.

questions.prompt: You are writing a quatrain with the rhyme scheme a b a b. Your first three lines already end with the words pine … flute … line … Which word must close the fourth line?
questions.explanation: In a b a b, line 4 answers line 2, so the last word has to rhyme with flute: mute does it. Wine is the trap, because it rhymes beautifully — with pine and line, which are the other pair, and using it there would turn the stanza into a b a a. Wood belongs to the same forest as pine but shares no sound with flute, and repeating flute itself is not a rhyme at all: a word never rhymes with itself.

questions.prompt: Your dictionary lists five senses for the word string. Which one is at work in this sentence: "A string of visitors waited under the arch."?

options.text: thin cord used for tying a parcel
the wire of a guitar or a violin
a queue of people or things
a set of beads on a single thread

questions.explanation: Nothing in the sentence is tied, played or threaded: what it shows is people standing one behind another, so string here means a queue, a line, a succession. It is a figurative use — the visitors are no more attached to one another than the shops in "a string of shops" are. That is the whole method with a word of several senses: read the sentence around it first, choose the sense that the context allows, then ask whether the use is literal or figurative.

questions.prompt: In the class discussion your teacher asks for an opinion AND the reason behind it, in one turn. Which answer does both?

options.text: I think the drum show is by far the best of the three.
I'd choose the drum show — you play it yourself.
The drum show costs £5 and the play £9.50.
Everybody in my class says the drum show is worth seeing.

questions.explanation: "I'd choose the drum show" is the opinion and "you play it yourself" is the reason, joined by a dash that costs nothing to write — one turn, two jobs done. Saying the drum show is by far the best is a strong opinion with nothing behind it, and strength is not a reason. Two ticket prices are facts anyone can check in the programme, so nobody could disagree with them. And reporting what everybody says hands the question to the class instead of answering it: an opinion has an owner.

questions.prompt: A leaflet lists Saturday's five events, but not in the order they happen: Family Talk 2.15 pm · Lunchtime Concert 12.30 pm · Doors open 9.45 am · Youth Arts Party 7.00 pm · Guided Tour 11.30 am. Put them back in the order of the day, from the first to the last.
questions.explanation: Sort the am times first, because they all come before midday: the doors open at 9.45 am and the guided tour follows at 11.30 am. Then the pm times, all after midday: the lunchtime concert at 12.30 pm — half an hour past midday, so an hour after the tour and not before it — then the family talk at 2.15 pm and the party at 7.00 pm. The figure 12.30 is the one that catches readers out, because 12 looks smaller than the 11 printed above it while the moment it names is later.
